generatedProse.concept-context: You often use another person's idea in your own words, by paraphrasing, rather than quoting it directly. That makes one rule easy to forget: a paraphrased idea still needs an in-text reference, the author and date, because the idea is someone else's even when the words are yours. Accuracy matters too, so build each reference from its parts rather than pasting one in, where errors and inconsistencies creep in.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two students use an author's idea, in their own words, in an essay.

Student A rewrites the author's point as a neat sentence of their own and moves on, giving no reference because nothing has been quoted directly. The sentence reads as Student A's own thinking. But the idea is the author's, and with no reference it is now presented as Student A's, the very thing referencing exists to prevent.

Student B also puts the author's point into their own words, but adds an in-text reference to the author and date. When Student B does quote directly, the exact words go in quotation marks with a page number. Quote or paraphrase, the idea is credited to the author either way.

Both students paraphrased accurately. Only Student B recognised that a paraphrase needs a reference just as a quotation does.
generatedProse.summary: Referencing accurately comes down to two habits: reference whenever you use someone else's idea - when you paraphrase as well as when you quote - and set each reference out carefully and consistently, rather than pasting in a ready-made one that may carry errors. You can now explain when an in-text reference is needed, tell an accurate reference from a flawed one, and choose the accurate way to reference a quotation or a paraphrase. With the purpose, the parts and the practice in place, you are ready to reference your own work with confidence.

check.body: In the worked example, what was the problem with Student A's paraphrase?

items.text: The idea was the author's, but with no reference it read as Student A's own.
The paraphrase was not written clearly enough.
It quoted too many of the author's exact words.
The paraphrase was shorter than the original.

feedback.correct: That's right. An unreferenced paraphrase presents the author's idea as Student A's own.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Think about what was missing from Student A's paraphrase.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Student A's paraphrase had no reference, so the author's idea read as Student A's own. Clarity, quoting and length were not the problem.
